Overview

Christchurch as a Business Centre

Christchurch is the largest city in the South Island and New Zealand's second-largest urban area. The city's territorial authority population was estimated at about 415,100 in June 2024, and city GDP was about NZ$31.5 billion in 2023, roughly 8.4 percent of the national total. Professional, scientific and technical services form the largest sector, followed by health care and manufacturing; the city is the country's second manufacturing centre after Auckland, with food processing a large share. Christchurch serves the wider Canterbury agricultural economy, and exports through its air and sea ports, Christchurch Airport and Lyttelton, were about NZ$9.3 billion in the year to February 2021. The city is also one of the five gateway cities for Antarctic operations.

The 2010 and 2011 Canterbury earthquakes shaped the city's commercial life for more than a decade. The February 2011 earthquake killed 185 people and led to the demolition of much of the central city, followed by one of the largest insurance and reconstruction programmes in New Zealand history. Organisations commission investigative work connected to Christchurch for that reason: insurers, owners and contractors in long-running claims, construction and development disputes, and lenders assessing builders and developers. Other triggers include due diligence on Canterbury manufacturers, food processors and agribusinesses, background checks on investment partners, and asset tracing against debtors whose property is held through companies and family trusts.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Christchurch

01

Earthquake insurance claims support

Fact development for insurers, property owners and their counsel in remaining Canterbury earthquake claims, including ownership and transaction history of damaged properties, repair and rebuild chronologies, contractor backgrounds and the involvement of claims advocates, assignees and purchasers of as-is properties.

02

Construction and rebuild disputes

Research into developers, builders, project managers and subcontractors active in the Christchurch rebuild, mapping related companies, prior insolvencies, litigation and adjudication history, and patterns where principals of failed construction companies reappear in new entities. Findings support lenders, principals and counsel.

03

Canterbury agribusiness due diligence

Ownership, directorship, litigation and reputational research on Canterbury farming groups, dairy and food processors and rural service businesses, supporting acquisitions, land and water-related transactions, lending, supply agreements and joint ventures where family trusts and closely held companies are common. Sources include Companies Office records and media.

04

Manufacturing and supplier integrity

Background checks on Christchurch manufacturers, distributors and their principals, and inquiries into procurement fraud, conflicts of interest and diversion of product, supporting internal investigations by employers and buyers relying on Canterbury suppliers. Work is scoped with the client's lawyers.

05

Asset tracing in the South Island

Identification of property, companies and business interests connected to a judgment or award debtor across Christchurch and Canterbury, built from lawful records, published judgments and open sources, so New Zealand counsel can assess freezing orders and enforcement.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Christchurch

High Court at Christchurch

The High Court sits in Christchurch and hears the South Island's significant commercial, insurance and property litigation, with appeals to the Court of Appeal. After the earthquakes it established the Christchurch High Court Earthquake List in May 2012, using mandatory first case management conferences, early fixed trial dates, priority for cases with precedent value and expert conferral protocols. As at September 2015, earthquake cases made up about 61 percent of the Christchurch High Court's caseload. The court has also heard representative actions by policyholders.

Earthquake claims legacy

By September 2016 the Earthquake Commission had received about 167,000 building claims and private insurers about 167,600 claims, with roughly NZ$18.9 billion paid by insurers. Claims continued to reach the courts well after that: in October 2024 the Court of Appeal decided Moorhouse Commercial Park v Vero, concerning commercial buildings damaged about 13 years earlier, and reporting noted that hundreds of claims remained unresolved. Disputes over repair standards, burden of proof and as-is property sales recur.

Council and regional records

Christchurch City Council is the territorial authority and holds rating, building consent and other property-related information for the city, while Environment Canterbury is the regional council. Council records can help establish the development and repair history of a site and the parties involved, alongside title and Companies Office records obtained through lawful channels. Requests are made through each council's own processes, and some information may be subject to privacy or official information rules.

Lyttelton, airport and Antarctic

Lyttelton is the main seaport serving Christchurch and Canterbury, and Christchurch Airport is New Zealand's second-busiest airport and the take-off point for the main US supply route to McMurdo Station and Scott Base. Together with Timaru, the region's ports carry a significant share of New Zealand's exports, so freight, logistics and export counterparties connected to the city are relevant to trade fraud and supply chain inquiries.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Christchurch

For matters touching Christchurch, TDSC first identifies the forum and the decision at stake: an insurance or construction proceeding in the High Court at Christchurch, an adjudication or arbitration, a transaction involving a Canterbury business, or enforcement against South Island assets. Many local disputes turn on decade-old events, so TDSC builds documented chronologies from Companies Office records, published judgments, council information, insolvency notices and archived media, reviewed under the Privacy Act 2020. Trust and company structures are mapped from lawful records, and formal searches and court steps are taken through New Zealand counsel. Where interviews or field inquiries are needed, TDSC coordinates private investigators licensed under New Zealand law. TDSC has no office in Christchurch.

TDSC has no office in Christchurch. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Christchurch: Frequently Asked Questions

Can TDSC help with an old Canterbury earthquake insurance claim?

Yes, as a consultant to the insurer, owner or their counsel. TDSC can reconstruct property ownership and transaction history, identify contractors and assessors involved in earlier repairs, and research parties who bought or took assignment of claims. Counsel decides how findings are used. TDSC does not assess building damage or give legal advice on policy coverage.

Does TDSC check builders and developers involved in the rebuild?

Yes. TDSC reviews Christchurch builders, developers and project companies for related entities, prior liquidations, litigation, adjudication history and media coverage, with attention to principals of failed companies who have started again under new names. Findings support procurement, lending and dispute strategy and do not replace formal licensing or credit checks.

What was the Christchurch Earthquake List?

It was a specialised High Court list established in May 2012 to manage the volume of civil claims arising from the Canterbury earthquakes. It used early case management conferences attended by the parties, fixed timetables, priority for precedent cases and protocols for experts to confer. Counsel should confirm current arrangements for any remaining earthquake proceedings.

Can TDSC trace assets held through Canterbury family trusts?

TDSC maps links between debtors, family trusts, companies and property in Canterbury using lawful records, published judgments and open sources. Trusts often hold farms and residential property, so a debtor may control assets without owning them personally. New Zealand counsel decides on title searches, freezing orders and enforcement steps based on the findings.

Does TDSC have an office or staff in Christchurch?

No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Christchurch or elsewhere in New Zealand. Engagements are managed from Nashville. Where a matter needs local inquiries, TDSC coordinates independent investigators holding the licence required under New Zealand law and works with the client's New Zealand lawyers under an agreed written scope.
